'''Oblivious HTTP''' ('''OHTTP''') is an [[Internet Engineering Task Force|IETF]] [[network protocol]] intended to enable anonymous [[HTTP]] transactions over the [[Internet]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |date=2025-03-19 |title=Oblivious HTTP Application Intermediation (ohai) |url=https://datatracker.ietf.org/wg/ohai/about/ |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) Datatracker}}</ref> Its goal is to allow a user to send an HTTP request to a [[web server]] without allowing any single entity to see both the content of the request and the sender's [[IP address]], since the IP address could be connected to the identity of the sender.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Sengupta |first1=Jayasree |title=How Resilient is QUIC to Security and Privacy Attacks? |date=2025-07-01 |eprint=2401.06657 |last2=Dey |first2=Debasmita |last3=Ferlin-Reiter |first3=Simone |last4=Ghosh |first4=Nirnay |last5=Bajpai |first5=Vaibhav |class=cs.CR }}</ref> OHTTP is documented in {{IETF RFC|9458}}, published in January 2024 by authors affiliated with [[Mozilla Corporation|Mozilla]] and [[Cloudflare]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last1=Thomson |first1=Martin |last2=Wood |first2=Christopher A. |date=January 2024 |title=RFC 9458: Oblivious HTTP |url=https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc9458.html |access-date=18 August 2025 |website=IETF |issn=2070-1721}}</ref> The RFC says "Oblivious HTTP is simpler and less costly than more robust systems, like {{Wikidata fallback link|Q136346840}} or [[Tor (network)|Tor]], which can provide stronger guarantees at higher operational costs."<ref name=":1" />

Some [[Technology company|technology companies]] and other [[Online service provider|online service providers]] have implemented OHTTP to improve [[Internet privacy]] for users, typically for specific use cases such as collecting [[Software metric|software metrics]] from client devices, collecting user data for [[targeted advertising]], or processing client requests for use of [[artificial intelligence]] services. The privacy protections in the OHTTP protocol rely on two separate entities handling different aspects of each client request, so service providers interested in deploying OHTTP generally partner with a different company. For example, Cloudflare and [[Fastly]] provide OHTTP relay services, and [[Apple Inc.|Apple]], [[Google]], [[Meta Platforms|Meta]], and Mozilla partner with one or both relay services for their OHTTP implementations.

== Mechanism ==
HTTP is the foundation of communication for the [[World Wide Web]]. By default, HTTP exposes a website user's [[IP address]] to the operator of the website, which may enable the operator to gather a [[Profiling (information science)|profile]] of information about the user.<ref name=":1" /> OHTTP is one of several protocols designed to protect the privacy of users making requests to web servers, using the principle of privacy partitioning (also called decoupling) to hide IP addresses.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last1=Schmitt |first1=Paul |last2=Iyengar |first2=Jana |last3=Wood |first3=Christopher |last4=Raghavan |first4=Barath |chapter=The decoupling principle: A practical privacy framework |date=2022-11-14 |title=Proceedings of the 21st ACM Workshop on Hot Topics in Networks |chapter-url=https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10388936 |series=HotNets '22 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=213–220 |doi=10.1145/3563766.3564112 |isbn=978-1-4503-9899-2}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Kühlewind |first1=Mirja |last2=Pauly |first2=Tommy |last3=Wood |first3=Christopher A. |date=2024-07-31 |title=RFC 9614: Partitioning as an Architecture for Privacy |url=https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9614/ |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) Datatracker |publisher=}}</ref> OHTTP is designed for simple transactions, such as sending [[web analytics]] information, rather than general-purpose web browsing.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Huston |first=Geoff |date=2023-03-23 |title=Hiding behind MASQUEs |url=https://blog.apnic.net/2023/03/23/hiding-behind-masques/ |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=APNIC Blog |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=McFadden |first=Mark |date=2024-07-02 |title=The Rise of the Intermediaries |url=https://dnsrf.org/blog/-the-rise-of-the-intermediaries |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=DNS Research Federation |language=en}}</ref> Most implementations of OHTTP involve an [[Application software|application]], such as a [[mobile app]], pre-configured to reach out to an OHTTP service for a particular type of transaction.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |last1=Pauly |first1=Tommy |last2=Reddy.K |first2=Tirumaleswar |date=2024-02-21 |title=RFC 9540: Discovery of Oblivious Services via Service Binding Records |url=https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9540/ |publisher=Internet Engineering Task Force}}</ref> 
[[File:Overview_of_Oblivious_HTTP.png|thumb|upright=1.3|Figure 1 from {{IETF RFC|9458}}: Overview of Oblivious HTTP]]
OHTTP protects user privacy by combining message [[encryption]] and specially-designed [[Proxy server|proxy servers]]. First, the client uses [[Hybrid cryptosystem|hybrid public key encryption (HPKE)]] to encapsulate the content of a HTTP request.<ref name=":2" /> Then, the client sends the encrypted request to a relay, which can collect the client IP address but cannot decrypt the message.<ref name=":1" /> The relay forwards the encrypted message to a gateway, which can decrypt the message but cannot find out the client IP address.<ref name=":1" /> The gateway sends the decrypted request to a server for processing.<ref name=":1" /> All traffic between the source, relay, gateway, and target server is sent over [[HTTPS]] to prevent third parties from analysing or intercepting the message contents.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=January 2025 |title=Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) explained |url=https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/ohttp-explained |access-date=18 August 2025 |website=Mozilla Support}}</ref> 

Since neither the relay nor gateway knows both the source IP address and the content of a request, the relay and gateway would need to collude to cross-correlate messages and de-anonymize them.<ref name=":2" /> If either of the operators is trustworthy, privacy is preserved. However, if both operators collude, they can compromise the privacy guarantees of OHTTP.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last1=Wood |first1=Christopher |last2=Hoyland |first2=Jonathan |date=2022-10-27 |title=Stronger than a promise: proving Oblivious HTTP privacy properties |url=https://blog.cloudflare.com/stronger-than-a-promise-proving-oblivious-http-privacy-properties/ |access-date=18 August 2025 |website=Cloudflare}}</ref> The gateway and target server are typically operated by the same organization, while the relay is typically operated by a different organization to prevent collusion.<ref name=":8" /> An analysis by [[NCC Group]] of an OHTTP implementation also noted that, to reduce risk of [[traffic analysis]] and other attacks, "Deployment of OHTTP requires careful management of [[Key (cryptography)|key]] rotation, [[rate limiting]], and tolerances against network delays."<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=2025-08-26 |title=Security and Privacy Assessment: WhatsApp Message Summarization Service |url=https://www.nccgroup.com/media/ymskbe40/ncc_group_metaplatforms_whatsapp-message_summarization_report_2025-08-27_v10.pdf |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=[[NCC Group]] |pages=8, 12-14, 25-26}}</ref>

Client applications configured to use OHTTP, such as applications designed to use OHTTP for certain [[API]] calls, do not need to try to find out whether OHTTP is available from a server.<ref name=":7" /> In other cases, if a server operator wants to tell clients that a service supports OHTTP, {{IETF RFC|9540}} (February 2024) defines an optional [[Domain Name System#Resource records|DNS resource record]] parameter.<ref name=":7" /> This mechanism enables a client to discover, after sending a DNS request, that they can send OHTTP requests, although the initial DNS request could expose the client's IP address to the server if not otherwise hidden.<ref name=":7" />

== Deployments ==
[[Cloudflare]] released an OHTTP relay service in 2022, called Privacy Gateway.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Galicer |first1=Mari |last2=Wood |first2=Christopher |date=2022-10-27 |title=Privacy Gateway: a privacy preserving proxy built on Internet standards |url=https://blog.cloudflare.com/building-privacy-into-internet-standards-and-how-to-make-your-app-more-private-today/ |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=The Cloudflare Blog |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> [[Flo (app)|Flo]], an app for tracking [[Menstrual cycle|menstrual cycles]], uses Cloudflare's OHTTP service to offer an "Anonymous Mode" that enables entering data into Flo without providing [[Personally identifiable information|personally identifying information]].<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Wetsman |first1=Nicole |last2=Faife |first2=Corin |date=2022-09-14 |title=Flo period tracker launches "Anonymous Mode" to fight abortion privacy concerns |url=https://www.theverge.com/2022/9/14/23351957/flo-period-tracker-privacy-anonymous-mode |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=The Verge |language=en-US}}</ref>

[[Google]] contracted with [[Fastly]] in 2023 to provide Google with an OHTTP relay to implement its experimental anonymous advertising technology.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-03-15 |title=Fastly wins major Google deal ahead of cookie death |url=https://www.thestack.technology/fastly-google-ohttp-relay-chrome-cookies/ |access-date=2025-03-04 |website=The Stack |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kuhn |first=Simon |date=2023-03-15 |title=Enabling privacy on the Internet with Oblivious HTTP |url=https://www.fastly.com/blog/enabling-privacy-on-the-internet-with-oblivious-http |access-date=2025-08-19 |website=Fastly |language=en}}</ref> Specifically, Google used OHTTP to help ensure [[K-anonymity|''k''-anonymity]] for its [[Privacy Sandbox]] initiative.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lee |first=Philip |date=2023-03-15 |title=Partnering with Fastly—Oblivious HTTP relay for FLEDGE's 𝑘-anonymity server |url=https://developer.chrome.com/blog/oblivious-http-for-k-anon-server-with-fastly |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=Chrome for Developers Blog |language=en}}</ref> Google also uses a Fastly OHTTP relay as part of its [[Google Safe Browsing]] service.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Bawa |first1=Jasika |last2=Lu |first2=Xinghui |last3=Li |first3=Jonathan |last4=Wozniak |first4=Alex |date=March 14, 2024 |title=Real-time, privacy-preserving URL protection |url=https://security.googleblog.com/2024/03/blog-post.html |access-date=2025-08-19 |website=Google Online Security Blog |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Amadeo |first=Ron |date=2024-03-15 |title=Google says Chrome's new real-time URL scanner won't invade your privacy |url=https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2024/03/google-says-chromes-new-real-time-url-scanner-wont-invade-your-privacy/ |access-date=2025-08-19 |website=Ars Technica |language=en}}</ref> Google offers a Safe Browsing Oblivious HTTP Gateway API that enables client applications, such as [[Web browser|web browsers]], to check whether a URL is on Google's list of unsafe websites without revealing the requester's IP address to Google.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-09-18 |title=Safe Browsing Oblivious HTTP Gateway API |url=https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/ohttp/reference |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=Google for Developers |language=en}}</ref>

In 2023, [[Mozilla Corporation|Mozilla]] started using Fastly's OHTTP relay service as part of collecting [[Firefox]] performance metrics without collecting identifying information about individual users.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Holley |first=Bobby |date=October 12, 2023 |title=Built for privacy: Partnering to deploy Oblivious HTTP and Prio in Firefox |url=https://blog.mozilla.org/en/firefox/partnership-ohttp-prio/ |access-date=2025-08-19 |website=Mozilla Distilled |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Iyengar |first=Jana |date=2023-10-12 |title=Firefox and Fastly take another step toward a privacy upgrade for the internet |url=https://www.fastly.com/blog/firefox-fastly-take-another-step-toward-security-upgrade |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=Fastly |language=en}}</ref>

As of 2024, [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] uses OHTTP in its Private Cloud Compute platform to conceal IP addresses associated with requests to [[Apple Intelligence]] tools.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024 |title=Private Cloud Compute Security Guide: Request Flow |url=https://security.apple.com/documentation/private-cloud-compute/requestflow |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250606092525/https://security.apple.com/documentation/private-cloud-compute/requestflow |archive-date=2025-06-06 |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=Apple Security Research |language=en-US }}</ref> Apple published support for OHTTP for its [[Swift (programming language)|Swift]] programming language in 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Benfield |first=Cory |date=2024-08-21 |title=Introducing Oblivious HTTP support in Swift |url=https://swift.org/blog/introducing-swift-nio-oblivious-http/ |access-date=2025-08-19 |website=Swift |publisher=Apple |language=en}}</ref> Apple said in 2025 that its Enhanced Visual Search uses OHTTP as part of its anonymization strategy.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 12, 2025 |title=About Enhanced Visual Search in Photos |url=https://support.apple.com/en-us/122033 |access-date=2025-03-04 |website=Apple Support |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Claburn |first=Thomas |date=2025-01-03 |title=Apple auto-opts everyone into having their photos analyzed by AI for landmarks |url=https://www.theregister.com/2025/01/03/apple_enhanced_visual_search/ |access-date=2025-09-21 |work=The Register}}</ref>

The [[Internet Security Research Group]] includes an OHTTP gateway in [[Divvi Up]], a service that enables subscribers to collect [[Software metric|software metrics]] from user devices while collecting minimal identifying information about users.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Geoghegan |first=Tim |date=2024-07-25 |title=Oblivious HTTP now available on Divvi Up |url=https://divviup.org/blog/ohttp-now-available/ |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=Divvi Up |publisher=Internet Security Research Group}}</ref>

As of 2025, [[Meta Platforms]] uses OHTTP in its "Private Processing" functionality for [[Meta AI]] tools, including to enable [[WhatsApp]] users to request summarization of messages without exposing the requester's IP address to Meta.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-04-29 |title=Building Private Processing for AI tools on WhatsApp |url=https://engineering.fb.com/2025/04/29/security/whatsapp-private-processing-ai-tools/ |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=Engineering at Meta |language=en-US}}</ref> This uses Fastly's OHTTP relay service.<ref name=":3" />

== Related technologies ==
{{Security protocol}}

An IETF working group, Oblivious HTTP Application Intermediation (OHAI), is responsible for working on OHTTP standards and collaborating with groups that work on related protocols.<ref name=":4" />

The [[Oblivious DNS over HTTPS]] (ODoH) protocol enables making [[Domain Name System|Domain Name System (DNS)]] requests using similar architectural principles as OHTTP ({{IETF RFC|9230}}, June 2022).<ref name=":0" />

Some people use [[VPN service|virtual private network (VPN) services]] to address privacy concerns, but this enables a single entity to see identifying information about the user and all of their activity that passes through the VPN.<ref name=":6" /> [[Tor (network)|Tor]] is a separate technology for protecting user privacy on the web by decoupling the sender from the receiver through at least three intermediate hops.<ref name=":6" />

[[MASQUE (protocol)|MASQUE]] (Multiplexed Application Substrate over [[QUIC]] Encryption) is a different set of protocols for improving the privacy of users making web requests.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Schinazi |first=David |date=2025-07-07 |title=The MASQUE Proxy |url=https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-schinazi-masque-proxy/ |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) Datatracker |publisher=}}</ref> It can be used for web browsing.<ref name=":5" /> For example, Apple's [[iCloud Private Relay]] service uses MASQUE.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nottingham |first=Mark |date=2022-12-30 |title=The state of HTTP in 2022 |url=https://blog.cloudflare.com/the-state-of-http-in-2022/ |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=The Cloudflare Blog |language=en}}</ref>
